sentences.text: The name Coelurus translates to "hollow tail," reflecting the animal's possession of hollow vertebrae in its tail region.
This small, bipedal carnivore stood approximately 0.7 meters tall at the hip and measured about 2.4 meters in total length.
Reconstructions indicate it had a long neck and torso, along with long, slender hindlimbs and a potentially small, slender skull.
Comparisons with the similar genus Ornitholestes show that Coelurus possessed a longer back and neck, as well as longer and thinner legs and feet.
The specific epithet "fragilis" was chosen because the scientist was impressed by the hollow interiors of the animal's thin-walled vertebrae.
When first described, the paleontologist considered the new genus to be an animal as long as a wolf and likely carnivorous.
The only valid species, C. fragilis, was described by the American naturalist Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879.
The main skeleton is nearly complete and is currently housed at the Peabody Museum of Natural History.
The type specimen was collected from gray sandstone and brown or green clay deposited during the Kimmeridgian stage of the Jurassic Period.
Coelurus was a small terrestrial carnivore that fed on small prey such as insects, mammals, and lizards.
Only one species, C. fragilis, is currently recognized as valid for the genus Coelurus despite six other species having been named historically.
Since the 1980s, Coelurus has generally been classified as a coelurosaurian with uncertain affinities that does not fit well into better-known Cretaceous clades.
Coelurus is the only known species of the extinct Coelurus genus, a ceratosaurian dinosaur.
Coelurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically between 155 and 152 million years ago, between the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages.
Coelurus lived in what is now North America.
It is debated whether Coelurus groups with compsognathids, as Oliver Rauhut proposed in 2003 but later studies failed to support.

There is a debate over whether Coelurus is a tyrannosauroid or a basal coelurosaur; Senter proposed it was a tyrannosauroid, but Turner et al. found it to be a basal coelurosaur more derived than tyrannosaurids.
Marsh was not certain that the animal was a dinosaur.
Some researchers interpret a Late Jurassic theropod vertebra formerly referred to Coelurus fragilis, along with a theropod astragalus and Calamosaurus foxi, as alvarezsauroids.
